passage: In the school's Creative Writing Club at 4 pm, Kunal read his story out loud to Samir, the club teacher. It was about a fox called Bhuri who lost her voice. "'I can't sing,' whispered Bhuri. 'Then we'll sing for you,' said the crows." Kunal's cheeks were warm and he kept his eyes on the page. Samir smiled. "That last line stayed with me. Is Bhuri sad?" Kunal thought. "A bit. But she has friends." Samir didn't ask whether it was about Kunal. He only said, "Stories can hold feelings. Thank you for sharing it." Kunal nodded, relieved, and added a poem about his dog. 🙂

qa.q: What was the fox in Kunal's story called?
qa.a: The fox was called Bhuri.

qa.q: What did Kunal's warm cheeks and eyes on the page suggest he felt, and what else might they mean?
qa.a: They suggest he felt shy and a little exposed reading his own work aloud. They might also mean excitement about sharing it.

qa.q: What could Samir do next to support Kunal's writing?
qa.a: Samir could keep responding to the story as a story, ask what happens next to Bhuri, and let Kunal decide whether to share anything about himself.

qa.q: What does Samir's decision not to ask 'Is it about you?' do for Kunal?
qa.a: It lets Kunal keep his story as fiction, so he can share feelings safely without being asked to explain or being pinned to a real event.

grounding: A child writes a story with dialogue and a poem; fiction can carry feelings, but the teacher treats it as a story and not literal fact.

passage: Ganga's little brother Farhan had a habit of writing in a notebook beside the fruit stall. Ganga, watching from the stall, saw him scribble a poem: "My cat Moti ran away / and the sky went grey." Then he wrote a story where a boy shouted at his teacher and flew away on a dragon. Their mother read over his shoulder and looked worried. "Did Farhan shout at his teacher?" she asked Ganga. Ganga shook her head. "No, it's a story, Ammi. He got a dragon in it." Farhan looked up, grinning, and read out the dragon's growl. Their mother relaxed and laughed.

qa.q: What was the name of the cat in Farhan's poem?
qa.a: The cat in Farhan's poem was named Moti.

qa.q: Why did Farhan's mother look worried, and what else could she have thought?
qa.a: She may have worried that the story meant Farhan really shouted at his teacher. Ganga's calm answer shows another reading: the story could just be imagination.

qa.q: What could Ganga or her mother do if they do want to know how Farhan feels about school?
qa.a: They could ask him gently about his day, without treating the dragon story as proof of what happened, and listen to what he says.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel when his mother asks whether he shouted at his teacher?
qa.a: He may feel misunderstood or surprised, since it was a made-up story. He seems proud enough of it to read out the dragon's growl.

grounding: A child writes stories and poems; fiction can carry real feelings, but a story is not proof that events or wishes are literal.

passage:
Monday: Bhavna wrote a story for English class about a puppy called Laddoo who wished his baby brother would float away on a balloon, so he could have all the biscuits. Her mother, Yamini, read it at the table and felt a small flicker of worry. Bhavna's own baby brother was asleep in the next room.
Wednesday: While folding clothes, Yamini asked lightly, "Do you ever feel like Laddoo about Chintu?"
Bhavna giggled. "Sometimes he takes my crayons. But Ma, it's a story. Puppies are greedy!" Then she added, "Laddoo brings him back at the end. Didn't you read the end?"
Yamini hadn't.
Saturday: Bhavna wrote a poem about Chintu sneezing like a tiny elephant. Yamini laughed, then stuck the story and the poem side by side on the fridge.

qa.q: What did Laddoo wish would happen to his baby brother?
qa.a: He wished his baby brother would float away on a balloon, so he could have all the biscuits.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she first read the story?
qa.a: Yamini felt a small flicker of worry that the story might show how Bhavna really felt about her baby brother.

qa.q: What did Yamini try that helped, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: She asked lightly instead of scolding or assuming, which let Bhavna explain; next time she could read the whole story first, since the ending changed its meaning.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see her mother's question?
qa.a: Bhavna seems amused rather than hurt, treating it as a funny mix-up, and a little surprised her mother missed the happy ending.

grounding: Across several days, a mother learns that her child's story about a jealous puppy carries real small feelings but is not a literal wish.

passage:
"Tenzin, come, sit. You're worried your story will get you in trouble? Listen to your Jomon Uncle. When I was in Class 4 in Kottayam, I wrote a poem about our dog Kittu called 'The Empty Bowl'. I wrote that the bowl sat empty every evening and his eyes were full of sorrow. My teacher read it and went very quiet. She thought Kittu had died! She even called my Amma after school to ask if I was all right.
But Kittu was only fat and greedy. His bowl was empty because he finished everything in ten seconds, and the sad eyes were for more rice.
Amma laughed so hard. Still, I was proud: my words had made someone feel something. A story can carry real feeling without being a true report."

qa.q: What was Jomon's poem about Kittu called?
qa.a: 'The Empty Bowl'.

qa.q: What was young Jomon feeling at the end of the story?
qa.a: He felt proud, because his words had made the teacher feel something strong, even though the poem was misunderstood.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story was wise, even though it turned out to be a mix-up?
qa.a: The teacher's choice to call Jomon's Amma the same day to check on him was wise, because a sad poem can sometimes signal real sadness, and checking cleared it up quickly.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt after learning Kittu was fine?
qa.a: The teacher probably felt relieved and a bit sheepish, and perhaps impressed that the poem had sounded so real.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood poem about his dog that carried strong feeling but was not proof of literal events.

passage:
The class poem contest had ten minutes left, and the room was noisy: chairs scraping, someone sharpening pencils nonstop. Shalini pressed her hands over her ears, then wrote fast.
"My cat Pepper is a pirate queen. She sails the sofa and steals my socks. I wish she would steal my homework and sail away forever."
Jyoti peeked over her shoulder and gasped. "You want your homework gone forever? Won't Miss be angry?"
Shalini snorted. "It's a poem! I just hate fractions. Pepper can't even open my bag."
Jyoti giggled. "Put in that she's scared of the vacuum cleaner."
"Pirate queens aren't scared of anything," Shalini said, but she added it anyway.
When the bell rang, the poem had six lines, and both of them were laughing.

qa.q: How many lines did the poem have when the bell rang?
qa.a: The poem had six lines.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she gasped at the homework line?
qa.a: Jyoti felt surprised and a little worried, taking the wish literally and fearing Miss would be angry.

qa.q: How did Shalini manage to finish despite the noise and time limit?
qa.a: She covered her ears, wrote quickly from a fun picture of her cat, and accepted Jyoti's idea instead of arguing, which kept her going.

qa.q: What would change if Miss read the homework line as a real plan?
qa.a: Miss might wrongly think Shalini was refusing homework, when the line only carries her real dislike of fractions in an imaginative way.

grounding: Under time pressure, a child writes a funny poem that carries a real feeling but is not a literal wish, and a friend first takes it literally.

passage: Ms Vasudha read Gurpreet's story twice in the staffroom. In it, a boy called Tiger-Jeet ran away from a castle where "the queen only shouted" and lived in a tree with his dog, Biscuit. The last line said, "He never went home again, and he was happy." Ms Vasudha didn't jump to conclusions. At break she crouched by Gurpreet's desk. "I loved Biscuit. Where did the castle come from?" Gurpreet grinned. "From the fort we saw on holiday. My mum shouts when I skip homework, but not like a queen. I just really want a dog." Ms Vasudha smiled. "So Biscuit might be the real wish." Gurpreet nodded and began a poem about a dog who waits by the door.

qa.q: What was the dog in Gurpreet's story called?
qa.a: Biscuit.

qa.q: What does Gurpreet's grin at the question suggest?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt proud and pleased that the story was noticed and seemed relaxed, not upset; the real feeling underneath was longing for a dog.

qa.q: What was wise about how Ms Vasudha asked?
qa.a: She praised a detail and asked where the idea came from, which let Gurpreet explain where fact ended and fiction began.

qa.q: How might Ms Vasudha have felt reading the last line?
qa.a: Ms Vasudha may have felt a flicker of concern, but she stayed calm and curious instead of assuming the story was literal.

grounding: It shows a child's story carrying a real wish while an adult checks gently rather than treating the fiction as proof of literal events.
